product.amstrad-pc9486.summary: The PC9000 range’s 486 combined a replaceable processor with tutorials for first-time PC users.
product.amstrad-pc9486.history: Amstrad introduced the PC9486 in early 1994 as part of the PC9000 range. The line covered professional work and home multimedia. The processor socket and tutorials addressed two priorities: making the system easier to upgrade and easier for beginners to use. BYTE reported UK prices from £849.99 and from £1,249.99 for the multimedia version. Computerwoche reported production in England.
product.amstrad-pc9486.technical.cpu: The ZIF socket made processor replacement easier. The documented range included a 25 MHz 486SX and 50 or 66 MHz 486DX2 models. Lawson distinguishes this AT model from the AT/PCI PC9486i.
product.amstrad-pc9486.technical.memory: The memory expansion limit varies between reviews. Joystick lists 48 MB and PC Review lists 64 MB. Both describe 4 MB as standard.
product.amstrad-pc9486.technical.video: Integrated graphics kept expansion slots available. Joystick describes a Cirrus Logic 5426 with 1 MB of video memory in the DX2-50 it tested.
product.amstrad-pc9486.technical.board: A surviving unit helps identify the board. Its owner documented UX486VIO-A Rev. 1.0 and UMC UM82C481BF and UM82C482AF chips.
product.amstrad-pc9486.warning: BIOS identified. BluMach boot validation pending.
product.amstrad-pc9486.technical.firmwar: The 64 KiB system image identifies the Amstrad PC9486 and carries the date 11/11/92. A memory dump from the same unit preserves another copy of the system block.
product.amstrad-pc9486.technical.verifie: The research cross-checked the commercial identity and compared the contents of the dumps. The BluMach status is research.
product.amstrad-pc9486.technical.limitat: The system blocks differ in four reset-vector bytes at FFF1–FFF4. The discrepancy needs investigation, followed by boot and peripheral validation.
